screens.title: Introduction to Serverless Deployment with AWS SAM & Serverless Framework
screens.narratorSegment: Serverless lets you write and deploy code without managing servers. In practice, that means you describe functions, events, and resources, and the cloud provider runs them on demand while you pay only for execution time. This chapter introduces AWS SAM, a CloudFormation extension that simplifies that description, and the Serverless Framework as an alternate multi-cloud tool. You will see how a simple template. yaml and a small Python handler can become a public A P I, and why SAM’s CLI flow — initialize, build, deploy — matters for packaging dependencies and creating consistent infrastructure-as-code. We will walk through a hands-on 'Hello World' example, explain the template syntax that maps to Lambda and A P I Gateway, and highlight common mistakes such as skipping the build step or lacking IAM permissions. By the end you should be able to read a SAM template, scaffold a project, run sam build and sam deploy --guided, and understand when you might choose the Serverless Framework instead. Think about what part of the deployment you currently manage manually; serverless is about shifting that responsibility to the platform so you can focus on the logic that creates value.

screens.title: What is Serverless Computing?
screens.narratorSegment: Serverless computing is an execution model where the cloud provider dynamically manages server allocation and scaling so developers focus on writing functions and services. Practically, that means you do not provision instances, patch operating systems, or manage auto-scaling groups — the provider handles those operational concerns. A concrete example is a Lambda function that runs in response to an HTTP request via A P I Gateway. You write the function code, describe it in a template, and the provider invokes it only when events occur. This model commonly pairs compute with services like A P I Gateway for HTTP endpoints, DynamoDB for persistent storage, and SQS for asynchronous messaging; together they form a serverless application. A common misconception is assuming serverless eliminates all operational responsibilities — you still design for cold starts, set appropriate timeouts and memory, and monitor for performance and cost. The key takeaway is that serverless shifts infrastructure management away from the developer, enabling faster iteration and pay-per-execution billing, but it does not remove the need to design resilient and observable systems. Consider where your application sees burst traffic or infrequent workloads — those patterns often benefit most from serverless.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Serverless shifts operational tasks to the cloud provider while letting you pay per execution and focus on code and events.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is Serverless Computing?
A cloud execution model that removes server management concerns and charges per execution.
Short definition

Serverless means the provider manages infrastructure, scaling, and runtime so you can deploy functions and services that respond to events.

Concrete example
A Python Lambda function returns JSON when API Gateway receives an HTTP GET request. You pay only when the function executes.
Common misconception
Serverless does not mean no operations. You still configure timeouts, memory, permissions, and monitoring to ensure correct behavior.
Key Takeaway

Serverless reduces operational overhead and enables pay-per-execution, but you must design for performance, costs, and observability.

Serverless components
Examples commonly used together
AWS Lambda
Stateless compute for event-driven code execution.
API Gateway
Expose HTTP endpoints that trigger functions.
DynamoDB
Serverless key-value store for persistence.
SQS
Queueing for asynchronous, resilient communication.
Think about which parts of your app would save time and cost by switching to event-driven serverless functions.

screens.title: AWS Serverless Application Model (SAM)
screens.narratorSegment: The AWS Serverless Application Model, or SAM, is an open-source framework that extends CloudFormation with shorthand resource types and syntactic sugar tailored for serverless patterns. Instead of writing verbose CloudFormation for Lambda functions, A P I Gateway configuration, and IAM roles, SAM lets you declare AWS::Serverless::Function resources with a compact Properties block. The Transform line in template. yaml — Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31 — tells CloudFormation to process SAM syntax and expand it into the full set of resources needed at deploy time. The SAM CLI takes the template, packages your code, and produces a deployable CloudFormation stack. A concrete benefit is that SAM automatically creates basic IAM roles and wiring between Lambda and A P I Gateway based on the Events you declare; you can still provide explicit roles or add policies if your function requires extra privileges. A common misconception is that SAM hides all CloudFormation details — it expands SAM shorthand into standard CloudFormation, so understanding generated resources helps with debugging and permission errors. The practical takeaway is that SAM accelerates serverless development while preserving the power and predictability of CloudFormation templates.

keyIdea.title: SAM Purpose
keyIdea.text: SAM provides concise serverless primitives that compile into full CloudFormation resources, giving simplicity plus CloudFormation's repeatability.

content.html:
Definition
AWS Serverless Application Model (SAM)
A CloudFormation extension that simplifies serverless resource definitions and packaging.
Transform directive

Including Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31 is essential; it instructs CloudFormation to expand SAM shorthand into the resources required to run your application.

Automatic wiring
Declare Events for a function and SAM will create the API Gateway integration and basic IAM role, reducing boilerplate.
When to inspect generated resources
If permissions fail or you need custom roles, examine the expanded CloudFormation template to see what SAM generated and extend it as needed.
SAM workflow
SAM CLI commands transform and deploy your application; below are the conceptual steps.
Define
Write template.yaml with Transform and Resources entries.
Build
Run sam build to collect code and dependencies into build artifacts.
Deploy
Use sam deploy --guided to create or update a CloudFormation stack from the packaged template.
Remember: SAM keeps CloudFormation's benefits while reducing the surface area for common serverless patterns.

screens.title: Understanding template.yaml
screens.narratorSegment: template. yaml is the central declarative file for SAM applications. At the top you specify AWSTemplateFormatVersion and the Transform line which enables SAM processing. The Resources block contains resource definitions such as AWS::Serverless::Function entries. Each Function has Properties like Handler, Runtime, CodeUri, MemorySize, and Timeout; these instruct SAM how to package the function and what runtime to use. The Events subsection defines triggers. For example, an Api event with Path and Method binds A P I Gateway to the function. A concrete example from this chapter shows a HelloWorldFunction with Type AWS::Serverless::Function, Handler app. lambda_handler, Runtime Python three.9, and an Events block defining an Api with Path /hello and Method get. Keep in mind that Method is typically uppercase in deployment: GET, POST, etc., and the Type for REST A P I triggers in SAM is Api. A common mistake is using an incorrect event Type like Http or wrong method casing; this will prevent CloudFormation from creating the intended A P I. The practical tip is to validate your template and run sam build so the code referenced by CodeUri is packaged and available at deploy time.

keyIdea.title: Template Anatomy
keyIdea.text: template.yaml uses Transform to enable SAM and Resources to define serverless functions and their triggers; Events map functions to API paths and methods.

content.html:
Definition
Understanding template.yaml
The YAML file that declares SAM resources, events, and packaging details.
Key fields explained
  • Transform: Enables SAM shorthand processing.
  • Resources: Contains AWS::Serverless::Function definitions.
  • Properties: Handler, Runtime, CodeUri, MemorySize, Timeout.
  • Events: Triggers such as Api with Path and Method.
Sample fragment
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31
Description: A simple serverless HTTP API with Python Lambda

Resources:
  HelloWorldFunction:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
    Properties:
      Handler: app.lambda_handler
      Runtime: python3.9
      CodeUri: hello_world/
      MemorySize: 128
      Timeout: 30
      Events:
        HelloWorld:
          Type: Api
          Properties:
            Path: /hello
            Method: get
Note: Keep Method casing consistent with SAM expectations; using Api as the Type maps to API Gateway integration.
Common Mistake

Incorrect event Type or forgetting sam build causes the deployed function to miss dependencies or fail to wire an API endpoint.

screens.title: Sample Python Lambda: app.py Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's look at the sample Python handler to understand what a Lambda function receives and returns. The example imports JSON, defines lambda_handler(event, context), prints the received event for logging, and returns a dictionary with statusCode, headers, and body containing a JSON-encoded message. This return shape matches what A P I Gateway expects when integrating with Lambda proxy responses: the status code signals success, headers set content type, and the body is a JSON string. A concrete run: when A P I Gateway forwards an HTTP GET to the function, event contains request context and path parameters; the function prints the event to logs and returns the greeting JSON. A common misconception is trying to return Python objects directly without JSON-encoding the body; A P I Gateway requires the body to be a string. Another practical point is that printing the event helps debugging in CloudWatch logs, but be mindful of PII in production. Key takeaway: write clear handler signatures, verify the response format expected by your A P I integration, and include simple logging to trace issues after deployment. Try adding a query parameter to the event and returning it in the response to see the request flow end-to-end.

keyIdea.title: Handler Contract
keyIdea.text: A Lambda handler receives event and context, logs input, and returns a response shaped for the API integration, typically with statusCode and JSON body.

content.html:
Process
Sample Python Lambda: app.py
Understand the handler signature and response format for API integration.
Handler pattern
A handler receives two arguments: event, which contains request data, and context, which provides runtime info. Logging the event is useful for debugging.
Misconception
Returning native Python objects without JSON-encoding the body will break API Gateway integrations. Always serialize the body to a string where required.
Try this

Add a query parameter and include it in the returned body to verify end-to-end request handling.

Example code
import json

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    """
    Sample Lambda function that returns a simple greeting.
    """
    print("Received event:", json.dumps(event))
    return {
        "statusCode": 200,
        "headers": {"Content-Type": "application/json"},
        "body": json.dumps({"message": "Hello from your Serverless API!"})
    }
This handler prints the event for CloudWatch logs, then returns a JSON body string with the greeting. Use statusCode and headers to control the HTTP response.

screens.title: SAM CLI Workflow: init → build → deploy
screens.narratorSegment: The SAM CLI orchestrates the local-to-cloud workflow in three main steps. First, sam init scaffolds a project using a template, choosing runtime and example code, which results in a template. yaml and sample function directory. That step gets you started but does not package dependencies. Second, sam build packages your application: it inspects template. yaml, installs dependencies for interpreted languages into a build artifact, and writes outputs to. aws-sam/build. This step is crucial when you rely on external libraries, because without it the deployed Lambda will miss modules. Third, sam deploy --guided walks you through stack name, region, and permissions; it packages the build artifacts, uploads them, and triggers CloudFormation to create or update your stack. A common mistake is deploying without running sam build first; this leads to runtime import errors. Another deployment failure mode is insufficient IAM permissions for the deploying user — create roles or grant privileges to allow creating Lambda, A P I Gateway, IAM roles, and CloudFormation stacks. The practical advice is to run the full sequence during your demo, confirm the A P I URL returned by deploy, and test with curl to validate the end-to-end flow.

keyIdea.text: sam init scaffolds, sam build packages code and dependencies, and sam deploy --guided creates a CloudFormation stack and deploys the API.

content.html:
Process Flow
SAM CLI Workflow: init → build → deploy
Commands prepare and publish serverless applications as CloudFormation stacks.
sam init
Scaffolds a starter project, including template.yaml and a sample function directory.
sam build
Packages code and dependencies into .aws-sam/build so deploy can upload a complete artifact.
sam deploy --guided
Guides you through stack configuration and then deploys a CloudFormation stack that provisions resources.
Pitfall: forgetting sam build is the leading cause of missing dependencies after deploy. Also verify you have permissions to create IAM roles and CloudFormation stacks before deploying in shared accounts.
Terminal-first notes
sam init
  # choose runtime, template, name
sam build
  # creates .aws-sam/build
sam deploy --guided
  # set stack name, region, allow role creation, save to samconfig.toml
Common Mistake

Deploying without running sam build causes missing modules and runtime errors in Lambda.

After deploy, copy the API URL from the CLI output and use curl to validate the JSON response.

screens.title: Hands-on: Deploying the 'Hello World' Serverless API
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on sequence follows the chapter activity for deploying a Hello World A P I. Begin by installing the SAM CLI and ensuring Docker is running if you plan local testing. Run sam init and select the quick start template for Python three.9 named my-serverless-api; this will create template. yaml and the hello_world directory with app dot P Y file. Inspect the project structure to see template. yaml and hello_world/app dot P Y file. Change into the project directory and run sam build; you should see a. aws-sam/build directory appear. Next run sam deploy --guided. The guided process prompts for a stack name, AWS region, whether to confirm changes before deploy, whether to allow SAM to create IAM roles, and whether to save settings to samconfig. toml. Accepting role creation simplifies one-time setup. When deploy finishes, the CLI prints the A P I Gateway endpoint for HelloWorldApi. Use curl with that URL to receive the JSON message. If you see missing-module errors after deployment, it usually means sam build was skipped or dependencies weren't present in CodeUri. Clean up by deleting the CloudFormation stack to avoid lingering resources. This demo cements the full lifecycle from local code to a public endpoint.

keyIdea.text: Run sam init, sam build, and sam deploy --guided; then test the API URL with curl and delete the stack when finished.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Deploying the 'Hello World' Serverless API
Terminal-first commands and expected outputs for a successful deployment.
Steps
sam init  # choose Python 3.9, Hello World, project name=my-serverless-api
cd my-serverless-api
sam build  # creates .aws-sam/build
sam deploy --guided
  # set stack name, region, allow role creation, save to samconfig.toml
# After deploy: copy API URL and run
curl https://.execute-api..amazonaws.com/Prod/hello
Expected: the CLI reports the API endpoint and curl returns the JSON {"message": "Hello from your Serverless API!"}.
Troubleshooting & cleanup
If the curl response fails, check CloudWatch logs for the Lambda function, confirm dependencies built into .aws-sam/build, and ensure deploy had permission to create roles. To remove resources:
aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name my-serverless-api-stack
Tip: Save answers to samconfig.toml during guided deploy to reproduce the same deploy later with sam deploy.
Key Takeaway

Follow the full sam init → sam build → sam deploy --guided flow to avoid missing artifacts and to produce a working API endpoint you can test with curl.

screens.title: SAM vs Serverless Framework
screens.narratorSegment: Both SAM and the Serverless Framework simplify serverless deployments, but they serve slightly different audiences and trade-offs. SAM is AWS-native: it is an extension of CloudFormation and compiles to familiar CloudFormation stacks. This gives SAM tight integration with AWS features and predictable CloudFormation-based deployments. The Serverless Framework is multi-cloud and uses serverless. yml to describe services; it has a rich plugin ecosystem and supports providers beyond AWS. A concrete example: for AWS-centric teams who want CloudFormation compatibility and fewer surprises with IAM, SAM is often the direct choice. For teams that need multi-cloud portability or community plugins for build pipelines, the Serverless Framework may be preferable. A common misconception is that Serverless Framework always hides CloudFormation — in AWS deployments it also generates CloudFormation or equivalent resources under the hood, so understanding generated resources remains important. The takeaway is not to view them as competitors alone but as complementary tools: for the AWS Certified Developer exam and AWS-native workflows, SAM is more directly relevant, while knowledge of Serverless Framework broadens your deployment toolbox. Common Assessment Questions
Practice reasoning about template syntax and CLI flow.
Question reasoning

screens.title: Permissions, Roles, and Common Deployment Failures
screens.narratorSegment: Permissions are a frequent source of deployment failure. When you run sam deploy --guided and allow SAM to create IAM roles, SAM will request permission to create roles that the functions need. If your deploying user lacks sufficient privileges, CloudFormation will fail to create roles, and the stack will roll back. A best practice is to either grant the deploying user rights to create roles or pre-create roles and reference them explicitly in template. yaml. Another common issue arises when SAM tries to upload artifacts to S3: the deploying user must have permissions to write to the target S3 bucket. During troubleshooting, examine the CloudFormation events and Lambda function creation logs to pinpoint permission denials. Also remember that resource creation failures during deploy often leave partially created stacks that should be deleted before retrying. In short, confirm IAM permissions for creating Lambda, A P I Gateway, IAM roles, and CloudFormation stacks, and ensure your sam deploy session is allowed to create necessary artifacts. Ask yourself: does the deploy user have full CloudFormation and IAM creation rights, or should you provide pre-created roles?

keyIdea.title: Permissions Tip
keyIdea.text: Deployment requires IAM permissions to create roles, Lambda functions, API Gateway, and to upload artifacts — verify deployer's rights before running deploy.

content.html:
Pro Tip
Permissions, Roles, and Deployment Failures
IAM permissions are often the root cause of failed SAM deploys; plan roles ahead of time when needed.
Checklist before deploy
  • Permission to create CloudFormation stacks.
  • Permission to create Lambda functions and IAM roles.
  • Permission to create and write to S3 buckets for artifacts.
Troubleshooting steps
Inspect CloudFormation events, check IAM errors, and delete failed stacks before retrying a corrected deployment.
Scenario
If your deploy fails with an IAM error, either give the deploying user the necessary permissions or provision a role with required policies and reference it in the function's Properties to avoid runtime failures.
Example
Allow SAM to create IAM roles during guided deploy, or supply an explicit Role ARN in template.yaml to control privileges.
Reflect: does your deployment account allow role creation, or do you need to coordinate with your cloud admin to run the deploy?

screens.title: Lifecycle: From Local Code to Deployed API
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the lifecycle helps you diagnose where failures occur. The timeline begins when you run sam build: SAM inspects template. yaml, installs or collects dependencies for the runtime, and produces artifacts under. aws-sam/build. Next, sam deploy packages those artifacts, uploads them to S3, and generates a CloudFormation change set. CloudFormation then creates or updates resources in the correct order: IAM roles and S3 buckets first, then Lambda functions, and finally A P I Gateway integrations. Once CloudFormation reports success, SAM prints the A P I endpoint for your function. If errors occur during stack creation, CloudFormation rolls back and you must review event logs to find the failed resource. An important detail is that sam build prepares the exact code that CloudFormation will reference; skipping it breaks the lifecycle. In practice, this timeline clarifies where to look for logs: build errors point to missing modules locally, deploy errors point to IAM or CloudFormation issues, and functional errors after deploy point to Lambda logs in CloudWatch. Ask yourself where in this timeline you would check first for a reported missing-module runtime error.

keyIdea.text: Build packages code, deploy uploads artifacts and runs CloudFormation, and CloudFormation creates roles, functions, and API Gateway integrations in order.

Process
Lifecycle: From Local Code to Deployed API
A step-by-step timeline of build, package, deploy, and runtime events to guide troubleshooting.
1. sam build
Packages code and dependencies into .aws-sam/build.
2. sam deploy
Uploads artifacts and creates a CloudFormation change set.
3. CloudFormation
Creates IAM roles, Lambda, and API Gateway in dependency order.
4. Verify & logs
Copy API URL, call it with curl, and inspect CloudWatch logs for function output.
This timeline shows where to check when problems arise: build for packaging issues, deploy for permission or packaging upload problems, and CloudWatch for runtime behavior.

fullNarratorScript:
Serverless lets you write and deploy code without managing servers. In practice, that means you describe functions, events, and resources, and the cloud provider runs them on demand while you pay only for execution time. This chapter introduces AWS SAM, a CloudFormation extension that simplifies that description, and the Serverless Framework as an alternate multi-cloud tool. You will see how a simple template. yaml and a small Python handler can become a public A P I, and why SAM’s CLI flow — initialize, build, deploy — matters for packaging dependencies and creating consistent infrastructure-as-code. We will walk through a hands-on 'Hello World' example, explain the template syntax that maps to Lambda and A P I Gateway, and highlight common mistakes such as skipping the build step or lacking IAM permissions. By the end you should be able to read a SAM template, scaffold a project, run sam build and sam deploy --guided, and understand when you might choose the Serverless Framework instead. Think about what part of the deployment you currently manage manually; serverless is about shifting that responsibility to the platform so you can focus on the logic that creates value.

These objectives focus on practical, testable skills for deploying serverless applications with SAM and understanding the Serverless Framework. First, you will understand serverless fundamentals: what 'serverless' manages for you and where it matters for cost and operations. Second, you will learn to use the SAM CLI to initialize, build, and deploy an application so your code and dependencies are packaged correctly. Third, you will read and author template. yaml entries that define Lambda functions, A P I events, and related resource properties such as handler, runtime, and CodeUri. Fourth, you'll deploy a simple serverless A P I that ties Lambda and A P I Gateway together and validate it with a curl call. Each objective pairs a concrete skill with why it matters, so you can both explain the architecture and reproduce the steps on your machine. Keep these goals in mind as we move through the examples and the guided terminal demo; they map directly to tasks you'll perform during a hands-on lab or on exam-style questions.

These practical objectives map directly to the hands-on deployment. You will initialize a SAM project using sam init so the starter project scaffold is created with template. yaml and the sample app. You will inspect template. yaml to identify the Transform line, the Resources block, and the AWS::Serverless::Function entries that implicitly create roles and A P I Gateway. You will run sam build to prepare code and dependencies into the. aws-sam/build artifact, avoiding runtime errors due to missing modules. You will then run sam deploy --guided to configure stack name, region, role creation consent, and save configuration to samconfig. toml. Finally, you will test the deployed A P I with curl or a browser to confirm the JSON payload. Each step demonstrates the end-to-end pipeline from local code to a public HTTP endpoint and reinforces the importance of packaging, permissions, and repeatability in serverless deployments.

Serverless computing is an execution model where the cloud provider dynamically manages server allocation and scaling so developers focus on writing functions and services. Practically, that means you do not provision instances, patch operating systems, or manage auto-scaling groups — the provider handles those operational concerns. A concrete example is a Lambda function that runs in response to an HTTP request via A P I Gateway. You write the function code, describe it in a template, and the provider invokes it only when events occur. This model commonly pairs compute with services like A P I Gateway for HTTP endpoints, DynamoDB for persistent storage, and SQS for asynchronous messaging; together they form a serverless application. A common misconception is assuming serverless eliminates all operational responsibilities — you still design for cold starts, set appropriate timeouts and memory, and monitor for performance and cost. The key takeaway is that serverless shifts infrastructure management away from the developer, enabling faster iteration and pay-per-execution billing, but it does not remove the need to design resilient and observable systems. Consider where your application sees burst traffic or infrequent workloads — those patterns often benefit most from serverless.

The AWS Serverless Application Model, or SAM, is an open-source framework that extends CloudFormation with shorthand resource types and syntactic sugar tailored for serverless patterns. Instead of writing verbose CloudFormation for Lambda functions, A P I Gateway configuration, and IAM roles, SAM lets you declare AWS::Serverless::Function resources with a compact Properties block. The Transform line in template. yaml — Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31 — tells CloudFormation to process SAM syntax and expand it into the full set of resources needed at deploy time. The SAM CLI takes the template, packages your code, and produces a deployable CloudFormation stack. A concrete benefit is that SAM automatically creates basic IAM roles and wiring between Lambda and A P I Gateway based on the Events you declare; you can still provide explicit roles or add policies if your function requires extra privileges. A common misconception is that SAM hides all CloudFormation details — it expands SAM shorthand into standard CloudFormation, so understanding generated resources helps with debugging and permission errors. The practical takeaway is that SAM accelerates serverless development while preserving the power and predictability of CloudFormation templates.

template. yaml is the central declarative file for SAM applications. At the top you specify AWSTemplateFormatVersion and the Transform line which enables SAM processing. The Resources block contains resource definitions such as AWS::Serverless::Function entries. Each Function has Properties like Handler, Runtime, CodeUri, MemorySize, and Timeout; these instruct SAM how to package the function and what runtime to use. The Events subsection defines triggers. For example, an Api event with Path and Method binds A P I Gateway to the function. A concrete example from this chapter shows a HelloWorldFunction with Type AWS::Serverless::Function, Handler app. lambda_handler, Runtime Python three.9, and an Events block defining an Api with Path /hello and Method get. Keep in mind that Method is typically uppercase in deployment: GET, POST, etc., and the Type for REST A P I triggers in SAM is Api. A common mistake is using an incorrect event Type like Http or wrong method casing; this will prevent CloudFormation from creating the intended A P I. The practical tip is to validate your template and run sam build so the code referenced by CodeUri is packaged and available at deploy time.

Let's look at the sample Python handler to understand what a Lambda function receives and returns. The example imports JSON, defines lambda_handler(event, context), prints the received event for logging, and returns a dictionary with statusCode, headers, and body containing a JSON-encoded message. This return shape matches what A P I Gateway expects when integrating with Lambda proxy responses: the status code signals success, headers set content type, and the body is a JSON string. A concrete run: when A P I Gateway forwards an HTTP GET to the function, event contains request context and path parameters; the function prints the event to logs and returns the greeting JSON. A common misconception is trying to return Python objects directly without JSON-encoding the body; A P I Gateway requires the body to be a string. Another practical point is that printing the event helps debugging in CloudWatch logs, but be mindful of PII in production. Key takeaway: write clear handler signatures, verify the response format expected by your A P I integration, and include simple logging to trace issues after deployment. Try adding a query parameter to the event and returning it in the response to see the request flow end-to-end.

The SAM CLI orchestrates the local-to-cloud workflow in three main steps. First, sam init scaffolds a project using a template, choosing runtime and example code, which results in a template. yaml and sample function directory. That step gets you started but does not package dependencies. Second, sam build packages your application: it inspects template. yaml, installs dependencies for interpreted languages into a build artifact, and writes outputs to. aws-sam/build. This step is crucial when you rely on external libraries, because without it the deployed Lambda will miss modules. Third, sam deploy --guided walks you through stack name, region, and permissions; it packages the build artifacts, uploads them, and triggers CloudFormation to create or update your stack. A common mistake is deploying without running sam build first; this leads to runtime import errors. The practical advice is to run the full sequence during your demo, confirm the A P I URL returned by deploy, and test with curl to validate the end-to-end flow.
